etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trenche. Doublet of tranche and traunch.

definitions.definition: A long, narrow ditch or hole dug in the ground.
(military) A narrow excavation as used in warfare, as a cover for besieging or emplaced forces.
(archaeology) A pit, usually rectangular with smooth walls and floor, excavated during an archaeological investigation.

quote.citation: 1999, April 24, Xiphias Gladius <ian@schultz.io.com>, "Re: trenchcoat mafia", ne.general.selected, Usenet:
quote.text: I was the first person in my high school to wear a trench and fedora constantly, and Ben was one of the first to wear a black trench.

quote.citation: 2007, Nina Garcia, The Little Black Book of Style, HarperCollins, as excerpted in Elle, October, page 138:
quote.text: A classic trench can work in any kind of weather and goes well with almost anything.

definitions.definition: (usually followed by upon) To invade, especially with regard to the rights or the exclusive authority of another; to encroach.

quote.text: Shee is the Judge, Thou Executioner, Or if thou needs would'st trench upon her power, Thou mightst have yet enjoy'd thy crueltie, With some more thrift, and more varietie.

quote.citation: 1832, [Isaac Taylor], Saturday Evening. […], London: Holdsworth and Ball, →OCLC:
quote.text: Does it not seem as if for a creature to challenge to itself a boundless attribute, were to trench upon the prerogative of the divine nature?

quote.citation: 1949, Charles Austin Beard, American Government and Politics, page 16:
quote.text: He could make what laws he pleased, as long as those laws did not trench upon property rights.

quote.citation: 2005, Carl von Clausewitz, J. J. Graham, On War, page 261:
quote.text: [O]ur ideas, therefore, must trench upon the province of tactics.

definitions.definition: (military, infantry) To excavate an elongated pit for protection of soldiers and or equipment, usually perpendicular to the line of sight toward the enemy.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: No more shall trenching war channel her fields.

quote.citation: 1715–1720, Homer, translated by Alexander Pope, “(please specify the book of the Iliad or chapter quoted from)”, in The Iliad of Homer, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintott […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Advanc'd upon the field there stood a moundOf earth congested, wall'd , and trench'd around

definitions.definition: (archaeology) To excavate an elongated and often narrow pit.
To have direction; to aim or tend.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Judicature”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: the reason and consequence thereof may trench to point of estate

definitions.definition: To cut; to form or shape by cutting; to make by incision, hewing, etc.

quote.citation: 1593, [William Shakespeare], Venus and Adonis, London:  […]  Richard Field, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The wide wound that the boar had trenched / In his soft flank.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: This weak impress of love is as a figure / Trenched in ice, which with an hour's heatDissolves to water, and doth lose its form.

definitions.definition: To cut furrows or ditches in.
To dig or cultivate very deeply, usually by digging parallel contiguous trenches in succession, filling each from the next.
